findings.title: Kickoff injuries are far more often head injuries
findings.summary: About 40% of serious kickoff injuries involved the head, versus 15% on other plays.
findings.notable_contrast: The 2025 kickoff rule raised live returns from 33% to 74% of kickoffs, so more players are exposed to that contact.

spec.title: Share of serious injuries that were head injuries

findings.title: One injury makes another more likely
findings.summary: Players already hurt earlier that season were injured again at a higher rate per snap.
findings.notable_contrast: The gap grew in recent seasons.

findings.title: Run plays are hard on ankles
findings.summary: Ankles made up a bigger share of injuries on runs than on any other play type.

spec.title: Share of injuries that were ankles

findings.title: Offensive linemen get hurt worse
findings.summary: When linemen are injured, it is more often serious.
findings.who_should_act: Team medical staff and line coaches

spec.title: Share of injuries that were serious

findings.title: Special teams is safer per play than offense
findings.summary: Even after fixing a parsing bug that undercounted punts, special teams had fewer serious injuries per play.

findings.title: The model is modest, and steady
findings.summary: It ranks risky situations better than chance, at about the same level every season since 2012.
findings.notable_contrast: Rule changes in 2018, 2020 and 2024 never clearly broke it. Late-game plays stayed a risk signal while kickoffs faded after the rule change.

data_quality_findings: Injured reserve hid 795 serious injuries from weekly reports until I added it as a source.
Play-by-play wording changed in 2024, which made it look like fewer players returned to games.
Offensive linemen are rarely named in play text (17% vs 47%), so 'returned to the game' had to be redefined.
The word 'Center' got parsed as a team name, creating 519 false player matches until fixed.
Public play text caught only 5 of the 35 kickoff concussions the NFL reported in 2025.
process: Joined four public nflverse datasets: play-by-play, rosters, injury reports and snap counts, 2009 to 2025.
Labeled which plays had an injury, then hid the play text from the model so it only saw pre-snap context.
Wrote down every comparison I'd test before looking at the results.
Trained the model on rolling windows of past seasons and tested each one on the following season, 120 models in all.
Refit one final model and put it in the browser, where its predictions match the Python version exactly.
nulls: Thursday games, turf, short rest, cold weather, rookies and the 2020 season with no preseason. None showed a reliable difference in either time period.
caveats: These are associations, not proof that a play type or condition causes injuries.
A recorded injury isn't every injury, and how injuries were written up changed over the years.
The model compares situations. It isn't a medical tool and can't predict a specific player's injury.
Independent project using public data. Not affiliated with the NFL or nflverse.
